```{r options, include = FALSE}

                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 4, width = 100)
```

Two questions can be asked of statistical software. Verification asks whether
the program computes what its method defines: the counts, the estimates, the
likelihood. Validation asks whether the method, as computed, describes the
process it is applied to. This article is about the first question for
transitiontrees. The package is an independent implementation of the
variable-order prediction suffix tree (Ron, Singer and Tishby, 1996), also
known as the variable length Markov chain (Bühlmann and Wyner, 1999). Its code
shares nothing with the reference implementation of the model in R, the PST
package (Gabadinho and Ritschard, 2016), which was archived on CRAN after
version 0.94.1.

The verification has two parts. The first runs in this article: on a small
bundled dataset, every quantity the tree estimates is computed again by hand
with a few lines of base R and compared with the package's output. The second
is an external equivalence suite that fits the same models with PST 0.94.1,
the markovchain package and the tna package and compares the results
quantity by quantity. The suite lives outside the package, in the source
repository, so that neither `R CMD check` nor a user needs the archived PST
package.

## What the tree estimates

For a context $s$, a sequence of up to `max_depth` states read oldest to
newest, let $N(s, a)$ be the number of times state $a$ follows $s$ in the
data and $N(s) = \sum_a N(s, a)$. Every position of every sequence is counted
once for the root and once for each preceding run of states up to
`max_depth`, so the first state of a sequence is counted only at the root and
the second at the root and at depth one. A context enters the tree when
$N(s) \ge$ `min_count`. Its maximum-likelihood next-state distribution is

$$\hat P(a \mid s) = N(s, a) / N(s).$$

The default `floor` smoother changes only a distribution in which some state
has a zero count. With $k$ states and floor $y$ (`ymin`), it becomes

$$\tilde P(a \mid s) = (1 - k\,y)\,\hat P(a \mid s) + y,$$

which is the rule used by PST. To predict a position, the tree uses the
longest context it holds among the states that precede it, and the
log-likelihood of a set of sequences is the sum, over all positions, of the
log-probability the tree gives to the observed state.

## Data

The hand computation uses the first ten learners of `trajectories`.

- **Sequence:** one row per learner.
- **Time:** columns `1` to `15`; trailing `NA`s mark the end of a shorter
  trajectory.
- **State:** `Active`, `Average` or `Disengaged`.

```{r data}
library(transitiontrees)
learners <- head(trajectories, 10)
learners
```

## Counting by hand

The hand computation needs two small functions written in base R, which use
nothing from the package. `count_by_hand()` lists, for every position of every
sequence, the root and each preceding run of up to `max_depth` states, and
tabulates the state that follows. It returns one row per context with its
total count and its count of each next state. `contexts_of()` turns the
pathway names of that table into histories that can be passed to `predict()`.

```{r helpers}
count_by_hand <- function(sequences, max_depth) {
  events <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(sequences)), function(i) {
    states <- unname(sequences[i, ])
    states <- states[!is.na(states)]
    per_depth <- lapply(seq.int(0L, max_depth), function(d) {
      positions <- seq_along(states)
      positions <- positions[positions > d]
      pathway <- vapply(positions, function(t) {
        if (d == 0L) "(start)" else
          paste(states[seq.int(t - d, t - 1L)], collapse = " -> ")
      }, character(1))
      data.frame(pathway = pathway, next_state = states[positions])
    })
    do.call(rbind, per_depth)
  })
  events <- do.call(rbind, events)
  counts <- table(events$pathway, events$next_state)
  data.frame(pathway = rownames(counts),
             count = as.integer(rowSums(counts)),
             as.data.frame.matrix(counts), row.names = NULL)
}

contexts_of <- function(hand) {
  lapply(hand$pathway, function(p) {
    if (identical(p, "(start)")) character(0) else
      strsplit(p, " -> ", fixed = TRUE)[[1L]]
  })
}
```

To count the contexts up to depth two, we call `count_by_hand()`.

```{r hand-counts}
hand <- count_by_hand(learners, max_depth = 2L)
hand
```

The ten learners contribute 147 observed states, all counted at the root. All
nine pairs of states occur as contexts of depth two, so the hand count has 13
contexts.

## Counts

To fit the tree that keeps every observed context, we call `context_tree()`
with `min_count = 1L`; `smoothing = list("floor", ymin = 0)` switches the
smoother off so that the probabilities are the raw maximum-likelihood
estimates.

```{r fit}
tree <- context_tree(learners, max_depth = 2L, min_count = 1L,
                     smoothing = list("floor", ymin = 0))
tree
```

To compare the counts, we merge the hand table with the tree's table from
`as.data.frame()` by pathway.

```{r compare-counts}
counts <- merge(subset(hand, select = c(pathway, count)),
                subset(as.data.frame(tree), select = c(pathway, count)),
                by = "pathway", suffixes = c("_hand", "_tree"))
counts
c(by_hand = nrow(hand), in_tree = n_nodes(tree), matched = nrow(counts))
with(counts, identical(count_hand, count_tree))
```

The tree holds the same 13 contexts as the hand count, and every count is
identical. The number of observations the tree reports, `nobs()`, equals the
root count.

```{r nobs}
nobs(tree)
```

## Maximum-likelihood probabilities

To compute the maximum-likelihood distributions by hand, we divide each next
state's count by the context's count. To obtain the tree's distributions, we
call `predict()` with each context as a history and `tidy = TRUE`.

```{r compare-mle}
mle_by_hand <- function(hand) {
  states <- setdiff(names(hand), c("pathway", "count"))
  data.frame(pathway = hand$pathway, hand[states] / hand$count)
}
by_hand <- mle_by_hand(hand)
fitted <- predict(tree, newdata = contexts_of(hand), tidy = TRUE)
subset(fitted, select = c(history, context, Active, Average, Disengaged))
identical(with(fitted, context), with(by_hand, pathway))
all.equal(subset(fitted, select = c(Active, Average, Disengaged)),
          subset(by_hand, select = c(Active, Average, Disengaged)),
          tolerance = 1e-12)
```

Every history is predicted from its own context, without back-off, and the
probabilities agree with the hand computation to within $10^{-12}$.

## Floor smoothing

Six of the hand-counted distributions contain a zero, for example
`Active -> Disengaged` (one `Active`, one `Disengaged`, no `Average`). To
check the default smoother, we apply the floor rule by hand with `ymin =
0.001` and compare it with a tree fitted with the default smoothing.

```{r compare-floor}
floor_by_hand <- function(probabilities, ymin) {
  states <- setdiff(names(probabilities), "pathway")
  p <- as.matrix(probabilities[states])
  k <- length(states)
  has_zero <- rowSums(p == 0) > 0
  p[has_zero, ] <- (1 - k * ymin) * p[has_zero, ] + ymin
  data.frame(pathway = probabilities$pathway, p)
}
smoothed_tree <- context_tree(learners, max_depth = 2L, min_count = 1L)
smoothed <- predict(smoothed_tree, newdata = contexts_of(hand), tidy = TRUE)
all.equal(subset(smoothed, select = c(Active, Average, Disengaged)),
          subset(floor_by_hand(by_hand, ymin = 0.001),
                 select = c(Active, Average, Disengaged)),
          tolerance = 1e-12)
```

## The log-likelihood

To compute the log-likelihood by hand, we score every position with the
hand-computed distribution of its longest preceding context and sum the
logarithms.

```{r compare-loglik}
loglik_by_hand <- function(sequences, max_depth, probabilities) {
  states_all <- setdiff(names(probabilities), "pathway")
  p <- as.matrix(probabilities[states_all])
  rownames(p) <- probabilities$pathway
  per_sequence <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(sequences)), function(i) {
    states <- unname(sequences[i, ])
    states <- states[!is.na(states)]
    sum(vapply(seq_along(states), function(t) {
      d <- min(t - 1L, max_depth)
      context <- if (d == 0L) "(start)" else
        paste(states[seq.int(t - d, t - 1L)], collapse = " -> ")
      log(p[context, states[t]])
    }, numeric(1)))
  }, numeric(1))
  sum(per_sequence)
}
loglik_by_hand(learners, max_depth = 2L, probabilities = by_hand)
logLik(tree)
all.equal(loglik_by_hand(learners, max_depth = 2L, probabilities = by_hand),
          as.numeric(logLik(tree)), tolerance = 1e-12)
```

## The same check on the full data

The same comparison can be run on all the bundled sequences at several
depths. `verify_by_hand()` combines the steps above and returns one row per
dataset and depth: the number of contexts found by hand and in the tree, and
the largest absolute differences in counts, probabilities and log-likelihood.

```{r verify-all}
verify_by_hand <- function(sequences, max_depth, label) {
  hand <- count_by_hand(sequences, max_depth)
  tree <- context_tree(sequences, max_depth = max_depth, min_count = 1L,
                       smoothing = list("floor", ymin = 0))
  tree_counts <- as.data.frame(tree)
  matched <- merge(hand, tree_counts, by = "pathway",
                   suffixes = c("_hand", "_tree"))
  by_hand <- mle_by_hand(hand)
  states <- setdiff(names(by_hand), "pathway")
  fitted <- predict(tree, newdata = contexts_of(hand), tidy = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    data = label, max_depth = max_depth,
    contexts_hand = nrow(hand), contexts_tree = n_nodes(tree),
    max_count_error = max(abs(matched$count_hand - matched$count_tree)),
    max_prob_error = max(abs(as.matrix(fitted[states]) -
                               as.matrix(by_hand[states]))),
    loglik_error = abs(loglik_by_hand(sequences, max_depth, by_hand) -
                         as.numeric(logLik(tree))))
}
checks <- Map(verify_by_hand,
              sequences = list(trajectories, trajectories, trajectories,
                               as.matrix(engagement), as.matrix(engagement)),
              max_depth = c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L),
              label = c("trajectories", "trajectories", "trajectories",
                        "engagement", "engagement"))
do.call(rbind, checks)
```

On the 136 non-empty trajectories and the 1,000 engagement sequences, at
every depth, the tree holds exactly the contexts found by hand, the counts
and the probabilities are identical, and the log-likelihoods differ by at
most $2 \times 10^{-11}$, the rounding error of summing thousands of
logarithms in a different order. (`as.matrix()` gives the engagement data
frame the same matrix form as `trajectories`, which the hand-count function
expects.)

## The external equivalence suite

The hand computation verifies the estimator against its definition. The
external suite verifies it against implementations written by other authors.
It is kept in `local_testing_and_equivalence/` in the source repository,
outside the built package, and runs only when the environment variable
`TRANSITREES_EQUIV_TESTS` is `true`. Its runner installs PST 0.94.1 from the
CRAN archive, installs the current source of transitiontrees, and runs three
test files.

**PST.** Thirty configurations are drawn at random with a fixed seed. Each
simulates first-order Markov sequences from a random transition matrix with
2 to 4 states, 50, 80 or 120 sequences of length 15, 20 or 25, and fits both
packages with `max_depth` from 2 to 4, `min_count` (`nmin` in PST) of 3, 5
or 8, and `ymin` of 0, 0.001 or 0.005. TraMineR builds the sequence object
that PST requires. Every configuration is compared on:

| transitiontrees | PST 0.94.1 | Criterion |
|---|---|---|
| node counts, all depths (`context_tree()`) | `pstree()` node counts | identical integers |
| node probabilities, all depths | `pstree()` node probabilities | absolute difference < $10^{-10}$ |
| set of contexts | `nodenames()` | identical sets |
| `nobs()` | `nobs()` | identical |
| `query_pathway()` | `query()` | absolute difference < $10^{-10}$ |
| per-position probabilities (`score_positions()`) | `predict(decomp = TRUE)` | absolute difference < $10^{-9}$ |
| `logLik()` | `logLik()` | relative difference < $10^{-10}$ |
| `plot_pruning()` distributions and counts | `query()` and node counts | < $10^{-10}$; identical |
| `plot_predictive(type = "logloss")` | $-\log_2$ of `predict(decomp = TRUE)` | absolute difference < $10^{-9}$ |
| `prune_tree(criterion = "G2")` | `prune(gain = "G2")` | measured agreement (below) |

**markovchain.** A tree of depth one without smoothing is a first-order
Markov chain. Its transition probabilities are compared with the
maximum-likelihood estimate of `markovchain::markovchainFit()` on three
simulated datasets with 2, 3 and 4 states (absolute difference
< $10^{-12}$).

**tna.** `prepare_input()`, which turns a long event log into sequences, is
compared with `tna::prepare_data()` over every combination of its arguments
(actor, time, order, action and the session time threshold) on three
long-format datasets from the Nestimate package, and an explicit session
column is checked to split sequences by actor and session.

### Results

The suites were last run on 2026-11-17 against transitiontrees 0.1.5 on
R 4.5.2 (Linux), with PST 0.94.1 installed from the CRAN archive,
markovchain from CRAN and tna 1.5.8.

| Suite | Tests (expectations) | Failures | Max abs count error | Max abs probability error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PST 0.94.1 | 10 (296) | 0 | 0 | 0 (log-loss: 4.4e-16) |
| markovchain | 1 (1) | 0 | not applicable | 0 |
| tna | 2 (422) | 0 | not applicable | not applicable |

The PST suite fits 30 random configurations (2 to 4 states, depth 2 to 4,
`min_count` of 3, 5 or 8 and `ymin` of 0, 0.001 or 0.005). Every shared context has the same
counts and probabilities, and the per-position predictive probabilities
agree exactly; the only non-zero difference is a log-loss difference of
4.4e-16, at the level of floating-point rounding. For the tna comparison
the contract is that both functions produce the same set of sequences for
each of the 420 argument combinations. Since tna 1.3.1, sessions built from
a time column are ordered numerically by actor, while `prepare_input()`
orders them as text, so the rows agree in order for 153 of the 420
combinations and as a set for all of them. Row order does not change a
fitted tree.

### What is not at parity

Some functions implement the package's own design and have no counterpart
in PST, so they are verified by the package's unit tests only.

- **Pruning.** `prune_tree(criterion = "G2")` and PST's `prune(gain = "G2")`
  use the same likelihood-ratio statistic but differ in two documented ways.
  transitiontrees compares $G^2$ with the chi-square critical value on
  $k - 1$ degrees of freedom; PST's worked example uses a cutoff equivalent to
  one degree of freedom. transitiontrees computes $G^2$ from the empirical
  child distribution, PST from the smoothed one, a difference of the order of
  `ymin` that can change a decision exactly at the cutoff. The suite measures
  the consequence: with PST's one-degree-of-freedom cutoff, the contexts
  transitiontrees keeps are always a subset of those PST keeps, and the two
  sets are identical when there are two states; with the cutoff matched to
  $k - 1$ degrees of freedom, the kept sets are identical in at least 85% of
  configurations, the remainder being decisions at the cutoff.
- **Distances, tuning and generation.** `tree_distance()` is a count-weighted
  symmetric Kullback-Leibler divergence, a different quantity from PST's
  distance. `tune_tree()` uses sequence-level k-fold cross-validation with
  its own fold assignment. `generate_sequences()` and `simulate()` consume
  random numbers differently from PST, so they can be compared in
  distribution only.
- **Smoothers.** The `laplace`, `kneser_ney`, `witten_bell` and
  `jelinek_mercer` smoothers have no PST counterpart. The `floor` smoother
  matches PST by default; `smoothing = list("floor", ymin = 0.001,
  rule = "cap")` selects the package's earlier clamp-and-renormalise rule,
  which differs from PST only at contexts with a zero count, by an amount of
  the order of `ymin`.
- **Reshaping.** `prepare_input()` produces the same set of sequences as
  `tna::prepare_data()`; their order can differ because the two functions
  sort session identifiers differently. Row order does not affect the fit.

## Running the suite

From the root of the source repository, with PST and the other reference
packages available, the suite runs with

```sh
TRANSITREES_EQUIV_TESTS=true Rscript local_testing_and_equivalence/run-equiv.R
```

which installs the reference packages that are missing (PST from the CRAN
archive), installs the package from source and prints one row per test with
its number of expectations, failures and errors.

```{r restore, include = FALSE}
options(old_options)
```
